Σπεύσας οὖν κατάβηθι· σήμερον γὰρ
ἐν τῷ οἴκῳσου δεῖ με μεῖναι. Ὢ χάριτος ἀφράστου! Ὢ φιλανθρωπίας ἀρρήτου!κάθαρτνου ὁ οἶκμεν ἡ τῶlumbh ει. Ὅπου γὰρ ξενίζεται ὁ Ἰησοῦς, πάντα πρὸς ἄμεινον μεταβάλλεται τρόπον. Ζακχαῖε, φησίν, σπεύσας κατάβηθι· σήμερον γὰρ ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ σου δεῖ με μεῖναι. Τί εἴπω; Ἡ οἰκία τοῦ τελώνου παράδεισος γέγονε. Ὃ γὰρ ἐπὶ τοῦ λῃστοῦ, τοῦτο καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ Ζακχαίου βλέπω· εἶπεν τῷ λῃστῇ· Σήμερον μετ' ἐμοῦ ἔσῃ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ καὶ λαβὼν αὐτὸν ἐκ τοῦ ξύλου εἰς τὸν παράδεισον εἰσήγαγεν· εἶπεν Ζακχαίῳ· Σήμερον ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ σου δεῖ με μεῖναι καὶ λαβὼν αὐτὸν εἰσῆλθεν πρὸ παραδείσου παράδεισον αὐτοῦ τὸν οἶκον ἐργασάμενος. Ὁ δὲ σπεύσας κατέβη καὶ προέδραμενωξεν ἀπηνω ἐκάλεσεν υἱὸς Ἀβραάμ . Ἀλλ' οἱ λαμοι οἱ ἐπὶ πού μεγογγύζειν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς λέγοντες ὅτι Παρὰ ἁμαρτωλῷ ἀνδρὶ εἰσῆλθεν καταλῦσαι. Ὦ καταφρονήσεως ἐργάται καὶ γεωργοὶ τῆς ῥᾳθυμίας! Ὑμεῖς τί ἐστε, δίκαιοι ἢ ἁμαρτωλοί; Οὐ πάντων ἀνθρώπων ἐστὲ μοχθηρότεροι; Πῶς οὖν παρ' ὑμῖν ἐσκήνωσεν Ἰησοῦς· πῶς παρ' ὑμῖν ἐτέχθη, ἐτράφη, ἠνδρειώθη, ἔπιεν, ἔφαγεν; Τί τὰ οἰκεῖα οὖν παρορῶντες τραύματα τὰ τοῦ πλησίον ἀνιχνεύετε πταίσματα; Ἄλλως δέ, διὰ τί ποτὲ μὲν ἁμαρτωλόν, ποτὲ δὲ δίκαιον τὸν Χριστὸν λέγετε; Ὅτε γὰρ τὸν ἐκ γεννητῆς ἐθεράπευσεν τυφλόν, ἁμαρτωλὸν αὐτὸν εἴπατε λέγοντες· ∆ὸς δόξαν τῷ θεῷ· ἡμεῖς γὰρ οἴδαμεν ὅτι ἁμαρτωλός ἐστιν, ὅτι λύει τὸ σάββατον. Νῦν ὅτε τὴν τοῦ τελώνου ὑπῆλθεν στέγην ὡς δίκαιον καὶ ἀναξίως ἁμαρτωλοῖς συνεσθίοντα διασύρετε ἁπλῶς. Ηὐλήσαμεν καὶ οὐκ ὠρχήσασθε· ἐθρηνήσαμεν ὑμῖν καὶ οὐκ ἐκόψασθε. Ἄν τε γὰρ θεραπεύσῃ τυφλόν, ἁμαρτωλὸν αὐτὸν λέγετε· ἄν τε ἁμαρτωλοῖς συμφάγῃ, διασύρετε ὡς ἀναξίως τοῖς ἁμαρτωλοῖς συνεσθίοντα. Τί οὖν; Μὴ θεραπεύσῃ ἐν σαββάτῳ τυφλόν, ἵνα μὴ ἁμαρτωλὸς νομισθῇ; μὴ φάγῃ μετὰ τελωνῶν, ἵνα δίκαιος ὑποπτευθῇ; Τί δὲ αἰτιᾶσθε αὐτόν, ὅτι παρὰ ἀνδρὶ ἁμαρτωλῷ εἰσῆλθεν καταλῦσαι; Καὶ ποῦ ἐχρῆν τεθῆναι τὸ φῶς ἢ ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ; Τὸ γὰρ φῶς ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ φαίνει καὶ ἡ σκοτία αὐτὸ οὐ κατέλαβεν. Ποῦ τὸνἰατρὸν ἐλθεῖν ἔδει; Οὐ προστρεχέτω κάμνοντας; Οὐ χρείαν γὰρ ἔχουσιν οἱ ἰσχύοντες ἰατροῦ, ἀλλ' οἱ κακῶς ἔχοντες. Ποῦ τὸν ἀμνὸν τοῦ θεοῦ ἐχρῆν φανῆναι; Οὐ πρὸς τοὺς τελώνας καὶ ἁμαρτωλούς, ἵνα τὸ φορτίον αὐτῶν ἀναλαβὼνκαταστήσειτίας; Μάτην λοιδορεῖτε· πεπλήρωται γὰρ ἐφ' ὑμῖν τὸ εἰρημένον ὅτι Πόρναι καὶ τελῶναι προάγουσιν ὑμᾶς εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶνφαρισαῖοι οἱlacuna sex linearumΣταθεὶς δὲ Ζακχαῖος εἶπεν πρὸς τὸν κύριον· ἰδοὺ τὰ ἡμίση τῶν ὑπαρχόντων μου δίδωμι τοῖς πτωχοῖς καὶ εἴ τινός τι ἐσυκοφάντησα, ἀποδίδωμι τετραπλοῦν. Οὐκέτι γὰρ πένητας ἀδικεῖν ἀνέχομαί σε τῶν πενήτων σκεπαστὴν οἴκοι δεξάμενος. Οὐκέτι ἐπτόημαι περὶ τὴν τῶν χρημάτων συλλογήν,πλοῦτον . Αἱ ἀλώπεκες φωλεοὺς ἔχουσι καὶ τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ κατασκηνώσεις, σὺ δὲ οὐκ ἔχεις ὅπου τὴν κεφαλὴν κλίνῃς. Οἰχέσθωσαν αὐλαὶ καὶ προαύλια, οἰκοδομῶν μεγαλουργίαι, λαμπροὶ καὶ περιφανεῖς οἶκοι. Ἀντὶ πάντων γὰρ τούτων ἀκένωτόν σου τῆς πενίας πλοῦτον ζητῶ. Ἀλλ' ἐπειδὴ ἐπὶ πλεῖον οὐ δύναμαι τῆς ψυχῆς Ζακχαίου διηγήσασθαι τὸν πλοῦτον, τῷ ἐν 4 ἀρεταῖς πλουτοῦντι πατρὶ τὸν λόγον καταλείψωμεν· ἀκόλουθον γὰρ τὸν φιλόξενον τοῦ φιλοξένου διηγήσασθαι τὰς ἀρετὰς πρὸς αἴνεσιν μὲν αὐτοῦ, στηριγμὸν δὲ ὑμῶν, στέφανον δὲ τῆς ἐκκλησίας, τιμὴν δὲ τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ᾧ ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν. 5
thought_title: Christ's lodging with Zacchaeus defended against the murmurers
orientation: Amphilochius is closing his homily on Zacchaeus, defending Christ's lodging with the tax collector against critics and praising Zacchaeus's restitution.
pass_a_gloss: So hurry, come down; for today in your house it is necessary for me to stay. O grace beyond telling! O love for humanity beyond speech! The house of the tax collector is made clean. For where Jesus is received as guest, everything changes for the better in manner. Zacchaeus, he says, hurry, come down; for today in your house it is necessary for me to stay. What shall I say? The house of the tax collector has become paradise. For what I see in the case of the thief, this I also see in the case of Zacchaeus; he said to the thief: Today you will be with me in paradise, and taking him from the tree he led him into paradise; he said to Zacchaeus: Today in your house it is necessary for me to stay, and taking him he entered, making his house a paradise before paradise. And he hurried and came down and ran ahead and received him and called him son of Abraham. But the murmurers who were always ready to murmur among themselves saying that Into the house of a sinful man he entered to lodge. O workers of contempt and farmers of idleness! What are you, righteous or sinners? Are you not more wicked than all people? How then did Jesus dwell among you; how among you was he born, raised, grew to manhood, drank, ate? Why then, overlooking your own wounds, do you track down the stumblings of your neighbor? And otherwise, why do you call Christ sometimes a sinner, sometimes righteous? For when he healed the man blind from birth, you called him a sinner saying: Give glory to God; for we know that this man is a sinner, because he breaks the sabbath. Now when he went under the roof of the tax collector, you disparage him simply as righteous and as one eating with sinners unworthily. We played the flute for you and you did not dance; we sang a dirge for you and you did not beat your breasts. For if he heals a blind man, you call him a sinner; and if he eats with sinners, you disparage him as one eating with sinners unworthily. What then? Should he not heal a blind man on the sabbath, so that he not be considered a sinner? Should he not eat with tax collectors, so that he be suspected as righteous? And why do you accuse him, that into the house of a sinful man he entered to lodge? And where was it necessary for the light to be placed except in the darkness? For the light shines in the darkness and the darkness did not overcome it. Where was it necessary for the physician to come? Does he not run to the sick? For those who are strong have no need of a physician, but those who are ill. Where was it necessary for the lamb of God to appear? Not to the tax collectors and sinners, so that taking up their burden he might restore them? In vain do you revile; for what was said has been fulfilled upon you, that Prostitutes and tax collectors go before you into the kingdom of heaven, Pharisees. [lacuna of six lines] And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord: Behold, half of my possessions I give to the poor, and if I have extorted anything from anyone, I repay fourfold. For no longer do I endure wronging the poor, having received you at home as protector of the poor. No longer am I terrified about the collection of money, wealth. No longer at the gates [lacuna] of travelers in human form [lacuna] having thought [lacuna] of previous things amnesty [lacuna] as his own [lacuna] was torn [lacuna] writings [lacuna of six lines] [lacuna of one line] I wish, being rich, he remained poor. Foxes have dens and the birds of the sky have nests, but you do not have where to lay your head. Let courts and forecourts go, the grand works of building, bright and conspicuous houses. For in place of all these I seek your inexhaustible wealth of poverty. But since I am not able to describe at greater length the wealth of Zacchaeus's soul, let us leave the word to the father who is rich in virtues; for it is fitting that the hospitable one describe the virtues of the hospitable one, for his praise, and for your strengthening, and for the crown of the church, and for the honor of Christ, to whom be the glory and the might forever and ever. Amen.

choices.term: Ὢ χάριτος ἀφράστου! Ὢ φιλανθρωπίας ἀρρήτου!
choices.english: O grace beyond telling! O love for humanity beyond speech!
choices.why: Keeps the exclamatory force and renders φιλανθρωπία with the glossary term 'love for humanity'.
rejected: O ineffable grace! O unspeakable kindness!

choices.english: making his house a paradise before paradise
choices.why: Preserves the paradox of the house becoming paradise and the phrase 'before paradise' (πρὸ παραδείσου).

choices.term: Ὦ καταφρονήσεως ἐργάται καὶ γεωργοὶ τῆς ῥᾳθυμίας!
choices.english: O workers of contempt and farmers of idleness!
choices.why: Keeps the agricultural metaphor of γεωργοί and the harsh tone of the address.
rejected: O laborers of scorn and cultivators of laziness!

choices.term: Ηὐλήσαμεν καὶ οὐκ ὠρχήσασθε· ἐθρηνήσαμεν ὑμῖν καὶ οὐκ ἐκόψασθε.
choices.english: We played the flute for you and you did not dance; we sang a dirge for you and you did not beat your breasts.
choices.why: Renders the quoted saying with its parallel structure and the specific action of breast-beating (κόπτομαι).
rejected: We piped and you did not dance; we wailed and you did not mourn.

choices.term: Οὐ χρείαν γὰρ ἔχουσιν οἱ ἰσχύοντες ἰατροῦ, ἀλλ' οἱ κακῶς ἔχοντες.
choices.english: For those who are strong have no need of a physician, but those who are ill.
choices.why: Keeps the contrast between the strong and the ill and the word 'physician' for ἰατρός.
rejected: The healthy do not need a doctor, but the sick.

choices.term: ἀκένωτόν σου τῆς πενίας πλοῦτον ζητῶ
choices.english: I seek your inexhaustible wealth of poverty
choices.why: Preserves the oxymoron of 'wealth of poverty' and the adjective 'inexhaustible' for ἀκένωτον.

pass_b_english: “Hurry and come down,” he says, “for today I must stay in your house” (Luke 19:5). O grace beyond telling! O love for humanity beyond speech! For wherever Jesus is received as a guest, everything is changed for the better.

“Zacchaeus,” he says, “hurry and come down, for today I must stay in your house.” What can I say? The tax collector’s house has become paradise. For what I see in the thief I see also in Zacchaeus. He said to the thief, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43), and taking him from the tree he brought him into paradise. He said to Zacchaeus, “Today I must stay in your house,” and taking him he entered, and by entering he made his house a paradise before paradise itself.
And Zacchaeus hurried down and ran ahead and received him joyfully. And Jesus called him a son of Abraham.
But the murmurers, who were always ready to murmur, said among themselves, “He has gone in to lodge with a sinful man” (Luke 19:7).

O workers of contempt and cultivators of idleness! What are you—righteous or sinners? Are you not more wicked than all people? How then did Jesus dwell among you? How was he born among you, raised among you, grow to manhood among you, drink among you, eat among you? Why do you overlook your own wounds and hunt out your neighbor’s stumbles?

And besides, why do you call Christ a sinner at one time and a righteous man at another? For when he healed the man born blind, you called him a sinner, saying, “Give glory to God; we know that this man is a sinner, because he breaks the Sabbath” (John 9:24). Now, when he has gone under the roof of a tax collector, you slander him as one who unworthily eats with sinners, as if he were a righteous man. We played the flute for you and you did not dance; we sang a dirge for you and you did not beat your breasts (Matthew 11:17). For if he heals a blind man, you call him a sinner; and if he eats with sinners, you slander him as one unworthily eating with sinners.

What then? Should he not heal a blind man on the Sabbath, so that he may not be thought a sinner? Should he not eat with tax collectors, so that he may not be suspected of being righteous? Why do you accuse him for going in to lodge with a sinful man? And where should the light have been placed except in the darkness? For the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it (John 1:5). Where should the physician have gone? Let him run to the sick! For those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill (Matthew 9:12). Where should the Lamb of God have appeared? Was it not to tax collectors and sinners, so that taking up their burden he might set them free? You revile him in vain. For what was spoken has been fulfilled in you: prostitutes and tax collectors go before you into the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 21:31), you Pharisees.

Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Look, half of my possessions I give to the poor, and if I have extorted anything from anyone, I repay it fourfold” (Luke 19:8). For I no longer endure wronging the poor, having received you, the shelter of the poor, into my house. I no longer tremble over the gathering of money, having found true wealth. I no longer stand at the gates watching travelers in human form. I have received amnesty for my former sins. Though rich, he remained in poverty. Foxes have holes and the birds of the air have nests, but you have nowhere to lay your head (Matthew 8:20). Let courts and porches go, the grand works of builders, bright and splendid houses. For in place of all these I seek your inexhaustible wealth hidden in poverty.

But since I cannot describe at greater length the wealth of Zacchaeus’s soul, let us leave the word to the Father who is rich in virtues. For it is fitting that the hospitable one describe the virtues of the hospitable one, for his praise, for your strengthening, for the crown of the church, and for the honor of Christ, to whom be glory and power forever and ever. Amen.
notes: The source text contains significant OCR damage and lacunae. The phrase 'κάθαρτνου ὁ οἶκμεν ἡ τῶlumbh ει' appears corrupted; I have glossed it as 'The house of the tax collector is made clean' based on context, but the exact wording is uncertain.

The passage 'Ὁ δὲ σπεύσας κατέβη καὶ προέδραμενωξεν ἀπηνω ἐκάλεσεν υἱὸς Ἀβραάμ' contains OCR corruption; I have glossed it as 'And he hurried and came down and ran ahead and received him and called him son of Abraham' based on the biblical narrative, but the exact verbs are uncertain.

There are two marked lacunae of six lines each, one lacuna of one line, and several shorter corrupted stretches in the section on Zacchaeus's speech about poverty; I have glossed only what is legible and marked the gaps.
The phrase 'φαρισαῖοι οἱlacuna sex linearum' indicates a lacuna of six lines after 'Pharisees'.

The phrase 'τηlacuna unius lineae θέλωπλούσιος ὢν πτωχεύσας διέμενε' contains a lacuna of one line; I have glossed the legible portion as 'I wish, being rich, he remained poor' but the connection is uncertain.

problems.fix: and ran ahead, and Jesus called him a son of Abraham.
problems.ruling: Greek says he called him son of Abraham; English adds ‘welcome him’ not in source

edits.old: Give glory to God; we know that this man is a sinner, because he breaks the Sabbath" (John 9:24).
edits.new: Give glory to God; we know that this man is a sinner, because he breaks the Sabbath" (John 9:24; cf. John 5:16).

fixed: The source says Jesus called Zacchaeus a son of Abraham (καὶ προέδραμενωξεν ἀπηνω ἐκάλεσεν υἱὸς Ἀβραάμ), so the English was corrected to make Jesus the subject of the calling.

The source passage is lacunose and corrupt (ἐν ἀνθρώπου μορφῇ ρονησάμενοςτῶν προλαβόν 5ν ἀμνηστείαν οὐον ὡςτὸν ἴδιον ετονδιερράγηγραφατῶν); 'amnesty of my former deeds' is an overinterpretation, so the English now marks the text as corrupt.
The source says 'being rich, he remained in poverty' (πλούσιος ὢν πτωχεύσας διέμενε), not 'chose to remain poor'; the English was corrected to reflect the ongoing state.
The source does not attribute the Sabbath-breaking reason to John 9:24; the citation was expanded to include John 5:16, where the Sabbath conflict is explicit.

previous_english: "Hurry, then, and come down, for today I must stay in your house" (Luke 19:5). O grace beyond telling! O love for humanity beyond speech! The house that receives Jesus is cleansed. For wherever Jesus is received as guest, everything changes for the better. "Zacchaeus," he says, "hurry and come down, for today I must stay in your house." What can I say? The tax collector's house has become paradise. For what I see in the thief, I see also in Zacchaeus. He said to the thief, "Today you will be with me in paradise" (Luke 23:43), and taking him from the tree he brought him into paradise. He said to Zacchaeus, "Today I must stay in your house," and taking him he entered, making his house a paradise before paradise. And Zacchaeus hurried down and ran ahead, and Jesus called him a son of Abraham.

But the murmurers, always ready to murmur, said among themselves, "He has gone in to lodge with a man who is a sinner." But I say to these murmurers: O idle troublemakers! What are you—righteous or sinners? Are you not more wicked than all people? How then did Jesus dwell among you? How was he born among you, raised among you, grown to manhood among you, drinking and eating among you? Why do you overlook your own wounds and track down your neighbor's stumblings? And besides, why do you call Christ a sinner at one moment and a righteous man at another? For when he healed the man born blind, you called him a sinner, saying, "Give glory to God; we know that this man is a sinner, because he breaks the Sabbath" (John 9:24; cf. John 5:16). Now, when he has gone under the roof of a tax collector, you disparage him as a righteous man, yet fault him for eating with sinners unworthily. As Christ said, "We played the flute for you and you did not dance; we sang a dirge for you and you did not beat your breasts" (Matthew 11:17). If he heals a blind man, you call him a sinner; if he eats with sinners, you disparage him as one who eats with sinners unworthily. What then? Should he not heal a blind man on the Sabbath, so that he is not thought a sinner? Should he not eat with tax collectors, so that he is suspected of being righteous? Why do you accuse him for going in to lodge with a man who is a sinner? Where should the light be placed except in the darkness? For the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it (John 1:5). Where should the physician go? Should he not run to the sick? For those who are strong have no need of a physician, but those who are ill (Matthew 9:12). Where should the Lamb of God appear? Should he not go to the tax collectors and sinners, so that taking up their burden he might restore them? You revile him in vain. For what was spoken has been fulfilled in you: "Tax collectors and prostitutes are entering the kingdom of God ahead of you" (Matthew 21:31).

And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord: "Look, I give half of my possessions to the poor, and if I have extorted anything from anyone, I repay it fourfold" (Luke 19:8). For I no longer endure wronging the poor, having received you, the shelter of the poor, into my house. I no longer tremble over the collection of money, for wealth... No longer do I lie in wait at the gates of travelers, scheming in human form... [text corrupt]

Being rich, he remained in poverty. "Foxes have holes and the birds of the air have nests, but you have nowhere to lay your head" (Matthew 8:20). Let courtyards and forecourts go, the grand works of builders, the shining and magnificent houses. In place of all these I seek your inexhaustible wealth of poverty. But since I cannot describe at greater length the wealth of Zacchaeus's soul, let us leave the word to the father who is rich in virtues. For it is fitting that the hospitable one should describe the virtues of the hospitable one—for his praise, for your strengthening, for the crown of the church, and for the honor of Christ, to whom be glory and power forever and ever. Amen.
